background.definition: Thyroid cancer is cancer originating in the thyroid gland. The four main types of thyroid cancer are papillary (85%), follicular (11%), medullary (2%-4%), and anaplastic (1%). Differentiated thyroid cancer, which includes papillary and follicular cancer, comprises more than 90% of all thyroid cancers.

list.listitem: The American Cancer Society estimates that there were 44,280 new cases of thyroid cancer in 2020, with 2200 deaths.
There is an increasing incidence of thyroid cancer in the United States predominantly because of increased detection of subclinical disease.
There were more than 360,000 men and women with thyroid cancer in the United States in 2004.
Thyroid cancer is the most common malignant endocrine tumor.
Thyroid cancer is the seventh most commonly diagnosed malignancy in women.
External radiation, especially to the head and neck, is a major risk factor for thyroid carcinoma.
A history of goiter or benign thyroid nodules appears to significantly increase the risk of developing thyroid carcinoma.

Inherited factors are associated with thyroid carcinoma in various familial cancer syndromes, including familial adenomatous polyposis syndrome, Cowden's disease, and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2.
A study found that the risk of thyroid cancer might be increased following exposure to the World Trade Center attack on 9/11/2001.

Thyroid cancer develops when a thyroid epithelial cell escapes from normal regulatory mechanisms and gains a selective growth advantage. This can result from mutations in both oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes.
Papillary thyroid carcinomas: rearrangements of RET or NTRK tyrosine kinases, or with activating mutations of RAS and BRAF resulting in carcinogenesis.
Follicular thyroid cancers: activating mutations of RAS or PAX8-PPARgamma1 fusion.
Medullary thyroid carcinomas: RET-activating mutations; a calcitonin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor originating from thyroid C cells.
Anaplastic thyroid carcinomas: inactivating mutations of tumor suppressor gene p53.

list.listitem: Screening is not recommended for the general population by the United States Preventive Services Task Force or British Thyroid Association.C
A family history should be taken for each patient and genetic counseling should be considered in the presence of a strong familial incidence of thyroid cancer. C
A meta-analysis of retrospective cohorts with over 11,000 patients established an association between obesity and worse prognostic features for thyroid cancer.
Genetic screening (germline RET testing) of family members is recommended for familial medullary thyroid carcinoma and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2. B
Prophylactic thyroidectomy should be performed on patients with RET mutations; the age at which surgery is recommended is based on risk category and laboratory and imaging findings.
The diagnosis of thyroid cancer is based on cytologic or histologic confirmation of malignancy. C
A history and physical examination to identify any potential risk for malignancy should be performed in all patients with thyroid nodules. C
High-resolution ultrasound is the most sensitive test available to detect thyroid nodules and the most accurate test for predicting the presence of malignant cells in thyroid lesions. B

Both initial size of a thyroid nodule and increase in size over time are not useful for differentiating benign from malignant nodules, so the use of annual ultrasound to follow-up nodules is unhelpful.
Fine needle aspiration of thyroid nodules to rule out malignancy should be based on ultrasonography features. B

list.listitem: See for classification and staging of differentiated thyroid carcinoma.
Most patients with differentiated thyroid cancer present with a thyroid nodule, but a few present with lymphadenopathy or, more rarely, with lung, bone, or brain metastases.

Historical features suggesting malignancy include age younger than 20 years or older than 70 years, male gender, prior head and neck irradiation, family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, and recent dysphagia, dysphonia, or cough. The male to female ratio is 3 to 1.

On physical examination, characteristics of malignancy may include firm consistency of nodule, irregular shape, fixation to underlying or overlying tissues, rapidly increasing size, and cervical lymphadenopathy.
ENT guidelines consider a neck mass that is at increased risk for malignancy if it has 1 or more of: fixation to adjacent tissues, firm consistency, size >1.5 cm, or ulceration of overlying skin.
Sensitivity and specificity for detecting thyroid malignancy by history and physical examination alone are 60% and 80%, respectively.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma usually presents as a thyroid nodule, although occasionally diarrhea, flushing, or ectopic Cushing's syndrome can be the mode of presentation due to hormonal secretion by the tumor cells. In most patients, the disease has already metastasized at time of presentation. Regional lymph node metastases are present in 50% of patients at diagnosis.

Most patients with anaplastic carcinoma of the thyroid present with a rapidly enlarging neck mass with pain, tenderness, and local compressive symptoms including dyspnea, dysphagia, hoarseness, and cough. Local or distant metastases are present in more than 90% of cases at presentation.
The chapter on thyroid nodule provides an overview of diagnostic testing to diagnose thyroid malignancy in patients with thyroid nodules.

High-resolution ultrasound is the most sensitive test available to detect thyroid nodules and most accurate test for predicting the presence of malignant cells in thyroid lesions. Although no single feature is diagnostic, ultrasound features associated with malignancy include microcalcifications, hypoechogenicity, irregular margins, and intranodular vascularity.

Fine needle aspiration (fine needle aspiration) is recommended to diagnose thyroid malignancy; the decision to biopsy is often based on size and/or ultrasonography features suggestive of malignancy. Repeatedly nondiagnostic aspirates require surgical excision or, at a minimum, close observation. If there are multiple nodules, those with the most suspicious appearance on ultrasound should be preferentially biopsied.

There are three sets of guidelines for thyroid nodule ultrasound findings that should lead to fine needle aspiration—Kim criteria (either marked hypoechogenicity, irregular or microlobulated margins, microcalcifications, or length greater than width), American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists (AACE) criteria (hypoechoic nodule with at least one additional feature) and the Society of Radiologists in Ultrasound (criteria based on size, calcifications, other components, and growth). One study found higher diagnostic accuracy with the Kim and AACE criteria (AROC 0.87 and 0.85, respectively vs. 0.55 for Society of Radiologists). The highest sensitivity was found with the Kim criteria and highest specificity with the AACE criteria.

The American College of Radiologists has a Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data Systems (TIRADS) to predict thyroid nodule risk of malignancy and there is a separate AI model and also British Thyroid Cancer Guidelines. A comparison of these 3 systems showed similar diagnostic performance with high sensitivity but lower specificity.
Thyroid nodule cytopathology should be reported using diagnostic groups described by the Bethesda System.
Although a low thyroid-stimulating hormone level somewhat reduces the likelihood of malignancy (LR = 0.23 if TSH <0.1 mU/L), it does not rule it out.
In patients with a thyroid nodule and elevated calcitonin, a peak pentagastrin-stimulated calcitonin >275 ng/L was useful in distinguishing medullary thyroid carcinoma from C-cell hyperplasia.

For patients with thyroid cancer, preoperative ultrasound to look for contralateral lobe involvement and cervical lymph nodes is recommended; the routine use of CT, MRI, PET, or serum thyroglobulin is not recommended.
Most patients with differentiated thyroid cancer present with a thyroid nodule. The diagnosis of thyroid cancer is based on cytologic or histologic confirmation of malignancy.

Please refer to chapter on evaluation of thyroid nodules for the approach to diagnostic testing in patients with thyroid nodules. The initial assessment of a thyroid nodule should include cervical ultrasound with classification using the TIRADS framework, and assessment of the patient's clinical risk factors.

Preoperative ultrasound of the contralateral lobe and cervical lymph nodes (central and lateral neck compartments) is recommended for all patients undergoing thyroidectomy for malignant cytologic findings on biopsy. Ultrasound-guided FNA of sonographically suspicious lymph nodes should be performed to confirm malignancy if this would change management. B

In addition to preoperative ultrasound, patients with suspected medullary thyroid carcinoma should have preoperative chest CT, neck CT, and 3-phase contrast enhanced multidetector liver CT or contrast-enhanced MRI when local lymph node metastases are detected (N1), or the serum calcitonin is >400 pg/mL.
For patients with suspected medullary thyroid carcinoma, include serum measurements of basal calcitonin, CEA, and calcium (albumin-corrected or ionized); and RET proto-oncogene analyses.
For most patients with thyroid cancer, the initial surgical procedure of choice is near-total or total thyroidectomy. A
Postoperative radioiodine ablation has been shown to significantly reduce disease recurrence and cause-specific mortality in high-risk patients. B
For patients with a differentiated low-risk thyroid cancer (papillary, follicular, or oncocytic/Hürthle-cell cancer), post-operative radioiodine offers no additional benefit. B
Initial TSH suppression to below 0.1 mU/L is recommended for high-risk patients, while maintenance of TSH between 0.1 and 0.5 mU/L is appropriate for low-risk patients. B
Local and distant metastatic disease recurrences should be managed by judicious use of radioiodine, surgery, or external beam radiation. B

Patients with well-differentiated thyroid cancer can be classified as high-risk, intermediate risk, and low-risk categories according to the tumor staging and other prognostic factors (older than 40 years, male, poorly differentiated, tumor size greater than 1.5 cm, extrathyroidal invasion, and metastatic spread).

Post-operative serum thyroglobulin may contribute to risk stratification in adjuvant therapy decision making. In addition, there is emerging evidence for BRAF mutational status correlating with prognosis.

For high- and intermediate-risk patients, treatment with supraphysiologic doses of levothyroxine is recommended to produce an initial suppression of TSH to <0.1 mU/L, which should be maintained indefinitely in patients with persistent disease.

For high-risk patients who are clinically and biochemically free of disease, a TSH level of 0.1 to 0.5 mU/L should be maintained for 5 to 10 years. In low-risk patients, an initial TSH level of 0.1 to 0.5 mU/L is recommended. When low-risk patients become disease free, TSH may be kept within the low normal range (0.3-2.0 mU/L).

The suppression of TSH to below normal limits is not recommended for patients with medullary thyroid carcinoma or anaplastic thyroid cancer; these patients should be placed on levothyroxine therapy postsurgically to maintain euthyroidism.

In patients with progressive thyroid cancer resistant to radioiodine, there are recent placebo-controlled RCTs showing some benefit from the use of kinase inhibitors in treating advanced/metastatic disease.These include vandetanib, sorafenib and lenvatinib.

Analysis of 21,870 patients in a national cancer database with intermediate risk papillary thyroid cancer showed significant benefit in overall survival from radioiodine treatment following resection.

Bisphosphonate or denosumab therapy may be considered for diffuse or symptomatic bone metastases from RAI-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer. Cytotoxic chemotherapy may be a further option in metastatic disease in patients unresponsive to kinase inhibitors, but data are limited on specific drug regimens.

For medullary thyroid cancer which is associated with RET mutation there is benefit from RET-inhibitor therapy with a recent randomised trial demonstrating increased progression free survival form selpercatinib.

For anaplastic thyroid cancer there are FDA approved genetic mutation-specific therapies. There is scope therefore for targetted therapy following tumour genetic analysis in patients suitable for systemic therapy, specifically if BRAF mutation or MET or ALK fusion.

Near-total or total thyroidectomy with central compartment lymph node dissection is recommended for most patients with well-differentiated thyroid cancer (see ). Radioactive iodine ablation of the remaining lobe in lieu of completion thyroidectomy is not recommended. Therapeutic central-compartment neck dissection should be performed in patients with clinically involved central or lateral neck lymph nodes and lateral compartment lymph node dissection should be performed in patients with biopsy proven metastatic lateral cervical lymphadenopathy.

For patients with a differentiated low-risk thyroid cancer (papillary, follicular, or oncocytic/Hürthle-cell cancer), post-operative radioiodine offers no additional benefit. A trial randomized 730 patients to radioiodine post-operatively or no radioiodine; at 3 years, with no difference in adverse functional, structural, or biologic events (95.9% vs 95.6% event-free).
Intraoperative nerve monitoring appears to be safe, although clinical trials have not shown a clear benefit in terms of long-term outcomes (NICE guidance).

Near-total or total thyroidectomy without prophylactic central neck dissection may be appropriate for small (T1 or T2), noninvasive, clinically node-negative papillary thyroid cancer and most follicular cancer.
There is no benefit to prophylactic central neck dissection in patients with node negative papillary thyroid cancer.
Prophylactic central-compartment neck dissection may be considered in patients with advanced primary papillary thyroid carcinoma with clinically uninvolved central neck lymph nodes.

Lobectomy is an option for patients with an indeterminate solitary nodule and for patients with a small (<1 cm), low-risk, isolated, intrathyroidal papillary carcinoma and no cervical nodal metastases.
For the low risk papillary thyroid microcarcinoma, emerging evidence suggests a role for active surveillance rather than immediate surgery.
For medullary thyroid carcinoma, total thyroidectomy with routine central compartment lymph node dissection is the initial treatment of choice.

Patients with ultrasound evidence of lymph node metastases in the lateral compartment should also undergo lateral compartment lymph node dissection; for patients with distant metastatic disease, less aggressive neck surgery may be appropriate to preserve speech, swallowing, and parathyroid function.

In patients with anaplastic thyroid cancer, surgery may not be indicated as disease may be advanced at the time of diagnosis. The decision to pursue aggressive therapy for metastatic anaplastic thyroid cancer should consider patient status and comorbidities, the extent of local invastion and distant metastases, and patient values. For those with localized disease (stage IVA), lobectomy with wide margins of adjacent soft tissue is the recommmended surgical approach. This may be followed by adjuvant radiotherapy with possible addition of adjuvant systemic therapy depening on extent of disease and fitness of patient. For those not pursuing surgery, options include primary chemoradiation vs. palliative radiotherapy, systemic therapy, or best supportive care.
Postoperative staging is recommended for all patients with differentiated thyroid cancer to improve prognostication and treatment planning and for entry into a cancer registry.

Postoperative radioiodine ablation is recommended for all patients with known distant metastases, gross extrathyroidal extension of the tumor regardless of tumor size, 1 to 4 cm tumors with lymph node metastases or other high risk features (when intermediate to high risk of recurrence or death is predicted), or for primary tumor size >4 cm even in the absence of other higher risk features.

Patients undergoing radioiodine ablation therapy can be prepared by levothyroxine withdrawal for at least 2 to 3 weeks with measurement of serum TSH to determine timing of testing or therapy (TSH >30 mU/L). Thyroxine therapy may be resumed on the second or third day after RAI administration.

External beam radiation is recommended for patients older than 45 years with grossly visible extrathyroidal disease that can not be completely removed with surgery and for patients with gross residual tumor in whom further surgery or RAI would likely be ineffective.

For patients with medullary thyroid cancer, postoperative radiotherapy to neck and mediastinum is indicated in those with extrathyroidal disease who can not undergo complete curative resection. The American Thyroid Association recommends external beam radiation therapy for patients with medullary thyroid cancer who have microscopic positive margin following surgery for moderate to high volume disease, in those with extra-nodal soft tissue extension of tumor when the post-operative serum calcitonin remains detectable in the absence of distant metastases, or for incompletely resected bone metastases.

For locally advanced anaplastic thyroid cancer, radiation and chemotherapy can be used for local control of disease, though long-term survival remains unaffected. Patients with Stage IVc anaplastic thyroid cancer have a very poor prognosis, and referral for palliative care should be considered, or possibly enrollment in a clinical trial.

Surgery is the management of choice for patients with recurrent metastatic disease confined to the neck, although radioiodine and external beam radiation can be considered if disease is nonresectable.

For pulmonary metastases, radioiodine therapy is recommended; this can be repeated every 6 to 12 months as long as the disease remains radioiodine avid. For radioiodine resistant pulmonary metastases, consider referral for clinical trials.

For cerebral metastases and isolated bone metastases, consider complete surgical resection first. For nonresectable metastases at these sites, radioiodine therapy and external beam radiation can be used when appropriate.
For patients undergoing radioiodine treatment, a low-iodine diet is recommended for the preceding 1 to 2 weeks.

The use of standard chemotherapeutic agents are not considered first line for patients with medullary thyroid cancer with progressive metastatic disease unresponsive to surgery and radiotherapy; rather, treatment with radiolabeled-molecules or enrollment in well-designed clinical trials should be considered.

The management of thyroid cancer is best delivered as part of a multidisciplinary team approach comprising an endocrinologist, thyroid surgeon, radiation oncologist, nuclear medicine physician, and primary care provider.

Transient (6%) or permanent (1%) damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve may occur following thyroidectomy. If voice dysfunction persists beyond 2 weeks after surgery, referral to an ear, nose and throat (ENT) specialist should be considered for evaluation and management.

Transient (5%-20%) or permanent (1%-10%) hypoparathyroidism can occur following thyroid surgery. Serum calcium should be monitored closely following surgery. If hypocalcemia is detected, supplementation with elemental calcium should be started. Calcitriol may be needed in addition to elemental calcium, if serum calcium does not improve or worsens on follow-up.
A randomised trial of weekly preoperative vitamin D for 4 weeks prior to surgery demonstrated a lower risk of symptomatic hypocalcemia post-operatively.
The overall 10-year survival rate for middle-aged adults with differentiated thyroid cancer is 80% to 90%; 5% to 20% of patients develop local recurrences and 10% to 5% have distant metastases. B
Using the TNM classification system, the 10-year survival rates for stages I, II, III, and IV medullary thyroid cancer are 100%, 93%, 71%, and 21%, respectively.
Serum thyroglobulin should be measured every 6 months to 12 months during follow-up of patients with differentiated thyroid cancer after initial surgery. B

A meta-analysis of 46 studies with over 2000 thyroid cancer patients demonstrated that E-cadherin expression correlates with stage and risk of lymph node metastases, and is a potential predictive factor for outcome.
Neck ultrasound should be performed annually during follow-up to detect local disease recurrences. B
The overall 10-year survival rate for middle-aged adults with differentiated thyroid cancer is 80% to 90%.

Although the recorded incidence of papillary thyroid cancer has increased, the death rate remains unchanged suggesting diagnosis in some who will progress only very slowly. This has been shown to be the case in older patients aged 40 to 50 years compared to the young adult group.
In a 6-year follow-up study of 327 patients with locally aggressive thyroid carcinoma, 92.5% of patients had complete remission and 7.8% had a recurrence.
Five percent to 20% of patients develop local or regional recurrences and 10% to 15% develop distant metastases.

Different staging methods have been proposed to assign patients to the high-risk or low-risk categories based on well-established prognostic factors, but TNM (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) and MACIS (Metastasis, Age, Completeness of resection, Invasion, and Size) systems are the most accepted.

Factors contributing to high risk include older age (older than 40 years), male gender, poorly differentiated histologic features, large tumor size (>1.5 cm), extrathyroidal invasion, and metastatic spread. Prognosis is also influenced by treatment.

A systematic review of 13 studies with 23,816 patients with differentiated thyroid cancer found little impact of minimal extrathyroid extension (mETE) on recurrence (2.2% without mETE and 3.5% with, p = 0.04). There was no significant impact on mortality (OR 0.5, 95% CI 0.11-2.21).
See for algorithm for follow-up of patients with differentiated thyroid cancer.
In one case series, ultrasound findings of a hypoechoic thyroidectomy bed with internal vascularity and a size >6 mm predicted recurrence.

Patients with medullary thyroid carcinoma should have serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels checked 2 to 3 months after surgery to detect the presence of residual disease. Those with undetectable levels should be followed at yearly intervals by physical examination and serum calcitonin and CEA levels.
Patients with medullary thyroid carcinoma and significantly elevated calcitonin levels should have imaging studies performed to localize local or metastatic disease.
Women should be advised to defer attempting conception for a minimum of 6 months (and men for 4 months) following radioiodine ablation or therapy.

Referring to a papillary thyroid cancer as a "papillary thyroid lesion" makes people less willing to accept treatment that requires lifelong medication, less willing to accept higher-cost treatment, and less likely to trade off side effects for benefit.
A nodule with malignant cytology should be monitored by ultrasound in pregnant women. If it grows significantly by 24 weeks of gestation, surgery can be performed at that point.
If it remains stable by mid-gestation or is diagnosed during the second half of pregnancy, surgery may be performed after delivery.
Radioiodine ablation or therapy must be avoided during pregnancy.
Suppressive levothyroxine therapy should continue during pregnancy with monitoring of TSH and free T4 during each trimester to ensure adequate TSH suppression.

The general principles of diagnosis and treatment of differentiated thyroid cancer in children are similar to those in adults. In one study of 83 consecutive children with papillary thyroid cancer, age was not associated with growth pattern or metastatic behavior.
Thyroid cancer is one of the most common subsequent malignancies in childhood cancer survivors, but this risk is lower than in the 1970's.

cell.label: Patient with well differentiated thyroid cancer. Was diagnosis benign disease after surgery?

Any of following: stage III or IV disease, age >45 years with stage II disease, or stage I disease with multiple foci, lymph node metastases, extrathyroidal extension, vascular invasion, or aggressive histology?
Levothyroxine to maintain TSH at <0.1 in high-risk patients and between 0.1 and 0.5 in low-risk patients.
All of the following present: size <1 cm, low-risk features, single focus, intrathyroidal tumor, no metastasis, no family history, and no history of radiation to head and neck.

feature.caption: TNM Classification and Staging System for Differentiated Thyroid Carcinoma.
feature.feature_body:
Tumor Definition
T1 Tumor size 2 cm or less
T2 Tumor size 2 cm to 4 cm
T3 Tumor size >4 cm, limited to thyroid or with minimal extrathyroidal extension
T4a Tumor of any size extending beyond the thyroid capsule to invade subcutaneous soft tissues, larynx, trachea, esophagus, or recurrent laryngeal nerve
T4b Tumor invades prevertebral fascia or encases carotid artery or mediastinal vessels
Tx Tumor size unknown, but without extrathyroidal invasion
Lymph nodes
N0 No metastatic lymph modes
N1a Metastases to pretracheal, paratracheal, and prelaryngeal lymph nodes
N1b Metastases to unilateral, bilateral, contralateral cervical or superior mediastinal nodes
Nx Nodes not assessed at surgery
Metastases
M0 No distant metastases
M1 Distant metastases
Mx Metastases not assessed
Stages: Patient younger than 45 years
Stage I Any T, any N, MO
Stage II Any T, any N, M1
Stages: Patient 45 years or older
Stage I T1, N0, M0
Stage II T2, N0, M0
Stage III T3, N0, M0
T1, N1a, M0
T2, N1a, M0
T3, N1a, M0
Stage IVA T4a, N0, M0
T1, N1b, M0
T2, N1b, M0
T3, N1b, M0
T4a, N1b, M0
Stage IVB T4b, any N, M0
Stage IVC Any T, any N, M1
